opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the core idea is that we want the baseline to reflect the situation the model is actually in. When you drop a model into a task, it has a lot of general knowledge and skill, but it doesn't have any of the specific context: it hasn't been working in that codebase for six months, it doesn't know the quirks of that particular system, it hasn't built up all the tacit knowledge about why things are set up the way they are. So if you compared it against someone who's been doing that exact job for years, you'd mostly be measuring the value of accumulated context, not the underlying capability we care about.

On the other hand, you don't want to use a random person off the street either, because then a lot of the time would just be someone learning what a Python virtual environment is, or how to read a stack trace. That isn't a meaningful comparison either. So the sweet spot is someone who has the relevant professional skills, like a competent software engineer or ML researcher, but who is coming to this particular task fresh. That's roughly analogous to the model having broad expertise but no situational familiarity.

There's also a practical, economic framing to it. A lot of what people care about is: what kinds of work could you hand to this system? A natural comparison is a skilled contractor or new hire who's capable but has to orient themselves. "How long would it take a competent new person to do this?" is a fairly intuitive unit, and it maps onto how people actually think about delegating work.

And then there's just measurement robustness. Task completion time for experts with deep context is very idiosyncratic, it depends heavily on exactly who you pick. Using skilled people who are new to the task gives you something more consistent and reproducible, which matters when you're trying to fit a trend across lots of tasks and lots of models.

I'd add the caveat that this does mean our time horizon numbers probably look somewhat different from what you'd get if you compared against people with full context on their own jobs. The models might seem less impressive relative to someone deeply embedded in a workplace, because that person is much faster at their own tasks. So when people translate our numbers into "how much of a real job can this automate," they should keep that gap in mind.

r001.rationale: The response says a model brings broad knowledge and skill but lacks task-specific context, making a skilled person new to the task an analogous baseline.

r002.rationale: It describes the model as having general knowledge and skill, but does not state that expertise available through public sources is not a bottleneck.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the core thing we're trying to measure is: what's the length of task, in human terms, that a model can complete reliably? And to do that you need some unit of "task length" that's actually comparable across tasks. Wall clock time for the model doesn't work, because models can run in parallel, they can be slow or fast depending on inference setup, and so on. So we want to express it as "how long would this take a person," and then you immediately have to answer: which person?

The reason we settled on someone with relevant expertise, but who's new to the specific task or codebase, is partly principled and partly practical.

The principled part is that this is the comparison that actually matters for the question of what AI can substitute for. If you're asking "can I hand this off to a model instead of a contractor or a new hire," the relevant comparison isn't the person who's been maintaining that codebase for five years and has all of it in their head. The model doesn't have that context either. It's getting dropped into a repo cold, reading the instructions, and trying to figure things out. So the fair baseline is someone with the general skills, like a competent software engineer or ML researcher, who's also walking in without the task-specific context. That's the situation the model is in.

If you instead used the expert who wrote the code, you'd get these incredibly short baseline times, because they'd just know where everything is, and the model would look terrible by comparison in a way that doesn't really reflect its usefulness. And if you went the other direction and used a total novice, you'd get absurdly long times, and the model would look superhuman on things that are actually pretty routine.

The practical part is that it's a baseline we can actually collect. We pay people to do the tasks, and we have to recruit them. We can recruit "skilled engineer who hasn't seen this before" at scale. We can't recruit "the specific person who built this system" for hundreds of tasks. And "new to the task" also keeps the measurements more consistent across baseliners, because you're not getting huge variance from how much prior familiarity each person happened to have.

There are obviously limitations. Our baseliners aren't always super motivated, they're doing it for a few hours, there's a learning curve, and so some of the human times are probably longer than what a really invested domain expert would get. We try to be upfront that these are noisy and that the absolute numbers aren't the thing to lean on. The thing that's actually robust is the trend: when you hold the baseline definition fixed over time, you see this pretty consistent doubling of the horizon length, and that holds up even if you perturb the baseline somewhat. So the choice of baseline shifts the intercept, but it doesn't really change the slope, and the slope is what we care most about.

r001.rationale: The response says the baseline is someone with general relevant skills who is new to the task or codebase, matching a model entering without task-specific context.

r002.rationale: The response discusses models lacking task-specific context, but does not state that they can draw on expertise from public sources or that this avoids an expertise bottleneck.

astra-6.text:
The idea is to measure how much work the task represents, rather than how much someone happens to know about that particular task already. So we want a human who has the relevant skills—you wouldn’t measure a programming task using someone who doesn’t know how to program—but who still has to figure out the specific problem.

If you use someone who’s been working in that codebase for years, they might know exactly where to make a change, and something that would otherwise take hours takes them five minutes. That makes the time estimate depend a lot on familiarity. Having someone with relevant expertise who’s new to the task gives us a more consistent baseline, and a closer comparison to an AI coming to the task with general capabilities but without that history.

r001.rationale: It says the baseline human has relevant skills but must figure out the specific problem, making the comparison closer to an AI arriving with general capabilities and without prior task history.

r002.rationale: It does not state that models can access expertise through public sources or that a lack of such expertise is not expected to bottleneck them.

sol-6.1.text:
The thing we’re trying to measure is how long an AI can carry out a task autonomously, and we need some way of describing how difficult or substantial that task is. The time it takes a human with the relevant skills is a useful yardstick.

We use someone who’s new to the particular task because familiarity can make an enormous difference. If you’ve already solved the problem, or you’ve spent years working in that codebase, you can be much faster because you have context that the model may not have. But we also don’t want to measure how long it takes someone to learn programming from scratch. So the idea is a person who has the relevant expertise, but still has to get oriented and figure out this particular problem.

It’s not a claim that there’s one definitive human completion time. It’s a practical reference point that lets us compare performance across tasks and models.

r001.rationale: The response says the baseline has relevant skills but is new to the particular task, and explains that prior task familiarity gives a human context the model may not have. This conveys the intended match to the model’s expected task knowledge.

r002.rationale: The response says the baseline should not need to learn programming from scratch, but does not state that models are expected to access expertise available through public sources or that lack of such expertise is not a bottleneck.
